children: AI is becoming moving from digital to become more physical - think human-shaped robots boxing up your online shopping order, instead of getting the AI chatbot of your choice to re-write your emails.

It feels like quite a different ballgame, and to be fair, commercial use is still very limited. After all, humanoid robots are highly complex and require many different parts - from software and semiconductors to motors and sensors.
According to Richard Farrell, a portfolio manager on the RBC Emerging Markets Equities team, two of those components form "the most important investment layer."
Firstly, so-called actuators, which Farrell described as "the muscles responsible for movement, balance and force." They're expected to be the most expensive components, he added.

"Within the actuator supply chain, reducers and screws emerge as the most compelling stock-picking opportunities, given their high average selling prices, technical entry barriers and import-substitution potential," Farrell said.

"Reducers" are basically gearboxes, and the screws, in this case, are devices that change the rotational movement of a motor into a linear motion. They might help a robot extend its elbow for example.
The second investment layer Farrell pointed out is sensors - which most of us probably have a slightly better idea of at least.
"Sensors form the robot’s nervous system, enabling perception and environmental awareness," he explains.

As humanoid adoption grows, Farrell notes, the sensor sector is shifting towards for example tactile sensors - which allow robots to feel touch, pressure and texture - and sensing skins - which are more or less the robotic equivalent to human skin.
"The key beneficiaries are likely to be major suppliers of critical components, especially sensors and actuators," Farrell concludes.
